newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain purchases of looted Nazi gold probed.
newsitem.headline: Spain purchases of looted Nazi gold probed.

text.p: Spain only returned a "symbolic" amount of the looted gold it bought from the Nazis during World War Two, the Nazi-hunting Simon Wiesenthal Centre's European director said on Thursday.

The Paris-based director Shimon Samuels was in Spain on Wednesday and Thursday investigating whether some of the gold passed through Spain and Portugal to Latin America and the Far East at the height of the war.
Between 1937 and 1944 alone, he said Spain bought 4,379 gold ingots weighing more than 65,000 kilograms, 2,738 ingots of it from Swiss National Bank.
"Spain gave back only eight ingots to the Tripartite Gold Commission as a symbolic gesture," Samuels told Reuters in a telephone interview.
At the end of the war, allied forces recovered 377 tonnes -- current value about $4 billion -- of looted gold and the Tripartite Gold Commission redistributed most of it.

The United States, France and Britain have agreed not to distribute the remaining $68 million of gold looted by the Nazis until they establish whether it could be given to Holocaust survivors, British diplomatic sources said earlier this month.
Samuels has asked them to return all the remaining gold to victims of Nazism, not to central banks as they have until now.
"What I want to underscore is that this gold did not get to the victims and their heirs," he told Spanish newspaper El Pais.
"My request is for all the victims, Jewish or not."
The Wiesenthal Centre, founded by Nazi hunter Simon Wiesenthal who captured Adolph Eichmann, will not ask Spain to return any more of the gold it bought from Nazis.
"We are not interested in that. We are only interested in uncovering the truth," Samuels said in the Reuter interview.
Samuels is investigating a golden triangle between Germany, Spain and Argentina. He indicated that art objects and shares, in addition to gold, also passed from Germany through Spain to Argentina.
He said he had uncovered clues pointing to such a triangle in documents at the Argentinian central bank, the U.S. Treasury and the French Finance Ministry.

One episode that aroused his suspicion was in August 1944 when the U.S. State Department told its embassy in Madrid that Credit Suisse of Zurich wanted to exchange 20 million Swiss francs in gold deposited in Argentina for bills via the Instituto Espanol de Moneda Extranjera (Spanish Foreign Currency Institute).
It was not clear if the transaction was completed.
Another incident which Samuels cited was a 1947 meeting between Argentinian President Domingo Peron's wife Eva and Hitler's banking minister Hjalmar Schacht in Spain.
He is also probing whether five German banks with branches in Madrid and subsidiaries in Argentina received Nazi gold.
Samuels suspects most of the gold which went to Latin America landed in Argentina but from there may have passed to other countries such as Chile.
Some of it went to Germans living in Argentina, where Nazis had taken refuge, and part of it was invested by Spain in the south American country, he said.
Samuels met Bank of Spain Governor Luis Angel Rojo on Wednesday to discuss the probe.
"They have promised me their collaboration," he said.
Rojo agreed to respond to a list of questions about German banks working in Spain and investments made in Spain with Nazi gold which Samuel will send later.

Newly discovered U.S. documents, revealed by U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato last month, showed the Swiss National Bank at the height of the war sent 280 truckloads of looted Nazi gold to Spain and Portugal in vehicles bearing neutral Switzerland's national emblem.
"It seems evident certain Spanish officials knew very well the illegal origin of the gold they bought," Samuels told El Pais.
"Any country which enjoyed the benefits of looted goods is an accomplice to these deeds."
Samuels left Spain on Wednesday for Lisbon, Portugal to pursue his inquiry.
